images.caption: Figure 2:Overview of Lang-SVG framework.Given an input image, we initialize a hierarchical Lang-SVG tree from multi-granularity and open-vocabulary segmentation masks. The tree is iteratively refined through differentiable SVG optimization, L1-SAM-Prompting to recover missing regions, and Add & Prune operations to add new leaves and prune redundant ones.

Figure 3:Image vectorization comparison.We compare our method with DiffVG[14], LIVE[20], and LIVSS[18]. Our SVGs achieve better reconstruction fidelity and semantic alignment with the ground-truth images, preserving object boundaries and fine-grained structural details.

Figure 4:Semantic SVG tagging.We leverage the tree context and Qwen3.5-27B to predict the unknown tags of SVGs shown on the left. For clearer visualization, we only render SVG components whose semantic tags belong to the target object. The results show that Lang-SVG enables fine-grained semantic reasoning, where the tail region is predicted as“bird tail”, while a smaller sub-region is further recognized as the“texture”of the bird tail.
Figure 5:SVG-style qualitative comparison.We compare SVGs produced by DiffVG[14], LIVE[20], SGLIVE[19], LIVSS[18], and our method.

Figure 6:More comparison results.We compare SVGs produced by DiffVG[14], LIVE[20], LIVSS[18], and our method. Our SVGs better align with the target images and preserve more coherent visual structures.

Figure 7:More comparison results under a lower point budget.We compare SVGs produced by DiffVG[14], LIVE[20], LIVSS[18], and our method. Our method produces SVGs with better visual fidelity and more coherent structure under the same point budget.
Figure 8:More semantic SVG tagging results.We show additional examples of semantic tags predicted for SVG components using our tree-guided semantic assignment.
